plot_extraction.response_text:
A writer struggling to create a Christmas story during wartime declares that Christmas has been destroyed by commerce, greed, and violence. Father Time appears and challenges him, then invites in Father Christmas, who has become ragged, frightened, and grief-stricken after years of wandering through a war-torn world. Traumatized by mines, machine guns, and the deaths of children, Father Christmas briefly regains his old warmth when given shelter, a fire, a drink, and the chance to mend a child’s broken toy. Yet the damaged books and undelivered gifts he carries remind him of children suffering and dying across Europe, and he collapses in despair.

Father Time tells the writer that everyone can help restore Christmas by shielding children, for now, from the hatred and horror of war and preserving for them its joy, charity, and kindness. He promises that the sacrifices of the dead may eventually produce a better world and a renewed peace. When the supernatural visitors vanish at dawn, the writer resolves to begin this work by mending his child’s broken toy horse.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story adopts the form of a conversational moral allegory, blending fantasy, social satire, sentiment, and wartime lament. Its central imaginative device is the personification of Father Time and Father Christmas, who appear as familiar supernatural figures in an otherwise ordinary domestic setting. Abstract historical forces are thereby made intimate and emotionally legible: Time is ancient, patient, and gently authoritative, while Christmas is represented as a traumatised, rain-soaked refugee whose physical deterioration embodies the damage inflicted by war.

The narration is first-person and retrospective, delivered by a self-conscious writer who is both participant and comic observer. The narrator occasionally addresses the reader directly, creating the manner of an informal fireside monologue. These addresses are teasing and intrusive rather than solemn: the narrator anticipates the reader’s anecdote, interrupts it, and insists on returning to his own experience. This mock intimacy establishes a genial raconteur’s voice and allows the story to move easily between supernatural reverie and conversational comedy.

The tone is deliberately mixed. It begins with whimsical uncanniness, develops through light irony and absurdist historical jokes, and then darkens into pathos as the consequences of war become explicit. Humour arises from incongruity: Father Time mistakes the narrator for someone under a hundred, ancient Egyptians prepare Christmas material in hieroglyphics, Babylonian jokes are baked in clay, and liquor supposedly kept “in case of illness” is exposed as an age-old excuse. Such comedy softens the allegorical machinery and makes the later suffering more forceful. Once Father Christmas enters, the humour remains present but becomes restorative rather than satirical, especially when warmth, drink, children, and the mending of a toy revive his old cheerfulness.

The diction combines plain, idiomatic speech with elevated, lyrical description. Dialogue is colloquial and full of contractions, interjections, repetitions, and exclamations: “Tut, tut,” “Pooh,” “Dear me,” and similar phrases give the characters distinctive theatrical voices. The descriptive passages use more ceremonious language, particularly when evoking the “thin curtain” of reality, the dying fire, the October wind, dawn, sacrifice, and the hoped-for renewal of the world. Archaic or old-fashioned expressions—“yule-tide,” “good cheer,” “pray, sir,” “I vow,” and “mummery”—support the traditional Christmas atmosphere and contrast with modern images of trenches, mines, machine guns, and hospitals.

Sentence structure is highly varied. Short exchanges create brisk comic timing, while longer, cumulative sentences build atmosphere or emotional intensity through coordinated clauses, repetitions, and lists. Dashes frequently mark interruptions, hesitations, afterthoughts, and sudden changes of direction. Repeated words and parallel phrases—“short—short,” “cold, sir, cold,” “all wet and torn,” and “Give me back my children”—produce an oral, incantatory rhythm. The prose often moves from a concrete detail to a broader symbolic meaning, as when damaged books become tokens of interrupted parental love or the broken toy horse becomes an emblem of a damaged world that can still be repaired.

The dialogue carries most of the exposition and argument. Rather than presenting its moral thesis directly at the outset, the story lets Father Time question the narrator’s cynicism and gradually guide him toward a renewed understanding of Christmas. Time speaks gently and often in whispers, functioning as mediator, philosopher, and stage manager. Father Christmas’s speech changes with his condition: at first it is timid and apologetic, then briefly hearty and authoritative when he repairs the toy, and finally anguished when memories of wounded and dying children overwhelm him. This modulation gives the allegorical figure a surprisingly human emotional arc.

Imagery is organised around strong oppositions: darkness and light, cold and warmth, storm and shelter, brokenness and repair, fear and hospitality, past cheer and present horror. The interior room, with its fire, books, pipes, chair, and toys, becomes a protected domestic space set against the violent world outside. Sound is especially important. Clock-ticking merges with Time’s murmuring; street noises become machine guns; wind becomes the voices of children; and the final speech dissolves into the sighing air. These ambiguous sounds keep the supernatural episode poised between dream, vision, and reality.

The structure is essentially dramatic and staged. It opens with the narrator alone at his table, introduces Father Time as a corrective voice, brings in Father Christmas as the visible evidence of the argument, allows a temporary revival beside the fire, then reaches an emotional crisis and a concluding moral commission. The vanishing of the visitors at dawn returns the narrative to the ordinary world, but a physical object—the broken horse—remains as a practical task. The ending therefore converts abstract sympathy into modest action: the narrator’s declaration, “I will mend this broken horse,” condenses the story’s ethic of care, preservation, and repair.

The pacing follows the tonal progression. Early dialogue is quick, playful, and digressive; Father Christmas’s entrance slows the narrative into detailed visual description; the fire-and-drink episode briefly accelerates into warmth and laughter; and the passages concerning war become increasingly repetitive, grave, and emotionally concentrated. The final speech by Father Time is the most explicitly didactic section, but its solemnity is prepared by the preceding imagery and characterisation.

The dominant themes are the endurance of humane traditions, the protection of childhood, the psychological devastation of war, and the moral value of kindness during catastrophe. Nostalgia is initially treated with some irony: the narrator imagines a perfect Victorian Christmas, while Time insists that the spirit of Christmas is far older and more persistent than any single historical style. The story ultimately rejects both commercial cynicism and passive longing for the past. Its preferred response is active tenderness—sheltering the vulnerable, preserving joy, practising charity, and repairing what can be repaired while awaiting a more peaceful world.

Overall, the style is that of an early twentieth-century Christmas fable shaped by the experience of modern warfare. It is accessible, theatrical, gently comic, and openly sentimental, with a clear moral purpose. Its most characteristic effect comes from placing homely humour beside extreme suffering: the same figure who asks for schnapps and mends a toy is haunted by trenches and dead children. That juxtaposition allows the story to defend innocence without ignoring history, and to end not in easy optimism but in a small, symbolic act of hope.

### THE REPAIR OF CHRISTMAS

I had been commanded to write a Christmas story.

That is a simple sentence, and it has the cheerful sound of an invitation to dinner; but those who have written Christmas stories know better. A Christmas story must contain snow, though the weather be wet; a fire, though coal be scarce; a child, preferably golden-haired; a miser who repents before the pudding; and some manifestation of Providence sufficiently surprising to be interesting but not so surprising as to alarm the family reader.

I had all these things except the story.

The fire had sunk to one red eye. Rain rattled upon the panes, and the wind came round the house like a creditor who knows you are at home. On the hearth-rug lay my little boy’s wooden horse. It had lost one wheel, its mane was scorched, and a crack ran through its painted body. He had brought it to me after supper.

“Can you mend him by Christmas morning?”

“Certainly,” I had said, with the magnificent confidence of a father who has not examined the damage.

Then he had gone to bed, leaving the horse with me; and I, leaving the horse untouched, sat down to mend Christmas.

I wrote at the top of a sheet:

“On Christmas Eve the snow lay white upon—”

Then I remembered that snow lay grey upon roads in wartime, and was speedily trampled into mud by boots, wheels, ambulances, and guns. I tore up the sheet.

I began again:

“Old Nathaniel Grudge had never loved a child—”

But I reflected that the world already contained too many men who had never loved a child, and that few of them could be cured by a pudding. I tore up that sheet also.

At last I threw down my pen.

“There is no Christmas,” I said aloud. “Commerce strangled it, greed sold the body, and war buried the remains.”

“Tut, tut,” said somebody behind me.

I turned.

An old gentleman sat in the high chair by the clock.

You will tell me, no doubt, that you once saw an old gentleman appear mysteriously in your aunt’s conservatory at Leeds, and that afterwards three spoons were missing. Pray reserve the anecdote. This was not your gentleman. Mine was very old indeed. His beard flowed over his breast like a white stream, and his robe seemed woven of smoke, moonlight, dust, and cobwebs. In one hand he held an hourglass. The sand in it did not fall steadily, but hurried, paused, climbed a little, and fell again, as though every grain had private business.

“You entered without knocking,” I said.

“So did you,” he answered.

“I beg your pardon?”

“Into the world.”

“That was not my fault.”

“It rarely is.”

He leaned toward the fire and warmed his transparent fingers above it.

“You’re Father Time, I suppose.”

“People call me so when they wish to blame me for their faces.”

I glanced at the clock. Its pendulum moved, yet made no sound. Instead I heard a faint whispering from the old man’s beard—summer leaves, bells, hoofbeats, crying babies, marching feet, wedding music, the shutting of doors.

“You said there is no Christmas,” he continued.

“I said it has been destroyed.”

“Dear me! And you are sure?”

“As sure as a man can be of anything after reading the newspapers.”

“A poor source of eternity.”

“It is gone,” I insisted. “It was eaten by shopkeepers long before the war. They wrapped it in gilt paper, priced it, advertised it, and sold it by the yard. Then came hatred, cannon, wire, submarines, bombs. What room is left for peace and goodwill?”

“Not much room,” he admitted. “But both have lived in smaller quarters.”

“I mean the true Christmas.”

“Ah, the true Christmas! Describe it.”

I did so. There was a country house with holly in every room, servants bearing steaming dishes, snow outside, a great log upon the hearth, children singing, poor people grateful for blankets, and all quarrels suspended until Boxing Day.

Father Time smiled.

“That is a very young Christmas.”

“It is the traditional one.”

“Traditional! My dear fellow, I remember when your traditional Christmas was a dangerous novelty. Before that there were midwinter fires on hills, and before those—well, never mind. A tribe beside an ice-bound river once shared its last haunch of venison with strangers. That was Christmas, though they had no word for it. An Egyptian clerk wrote a seasonal tale in hieroglyphics and complained that the editor altered the ending. A Babylonian humorist baked jokes upon clay tablets.”

“Were they good jokes?”

“No. Humour improves more slowly than weapons.”

He peered at my blank paper.

“And now you declare the festival dead because you cannot begin a story.”

“I declare it dead because the world has murdered it.”

“No,” he said softly. “The world has wounded it.”

The wind struck the window. Somewhere in the street a motor backfired, and I started; the sound had been too much like a rifle.

Father Time looked toward the door.

“He is outside.”

“Who?”

“The witness for the defence.”

There came a timid knock.

It was not the knock of a supernatural person. It was the knock of a beggar who fears refusal, of a traveller uncertain of his welcome, of one who has knocked at many doors and seen curtains drawn quickly across warm windows.

“Open,” said Father Time.

I opened.

A figure stood upon the step beneath the rain.

At first I took him for some ruined actor escaped from a provincial pantomime. He wore a red coat, but it had faded to the colour of dried blood and hung in strips at the hem. The fur was grey with mud. One boot was bound with wire, the other with a bandage. His cap drooped over his eyes, and from beneath it streamed wet white hair. A sack sagged across his shoulders, patched with canvas, hospital cloth, and what looked horribly like the torn sleeve of a child’s coat.

He lifted his face.

I knew him then, though the cheeks were hollow, the lips blue, and the eyes—those famous merry eyes—darted from hedge to window, from window to rooftop, watching for dangers no one else could see.

“May I come in, sir?” he asked. “Only for a moment. I’ll leave if there’s trouble.”

“Come in, Father Christmas.”

He flinched at the name.

“Hush! Not so loud.”

The old man by the clock rose.

“Welcome, Nicholas.”

Father Christmas stared at him, and some of the fear left his face.

“Time! Is it truly you?”

“It usually is.”

They embraced. Father Christmas trembled so violently that drops flew from his beard.

“He is frozen,” said Time. “Do something.”

This was unfair. One expects apparitions to manage their own temperatures. Still, I stirred the coals, added the last decent lump from the scuttle, and drew the high chair close. Father Christmas sat with an apologetic heaviness. Water gathered beneath him.

“My wife will be delighted,” I murmured.

“She has forgiven worse,” said Father Time. “I remember the blue vase.”

I ignored this indecent knowledge of domestic history and fetched a towel.

When I tried to take Father Christmas’s sack, he clutched it.

“No! Don’t touch!”

“I only meant to put it down.”

“Wires,” he whispered. “They fasten things to wires. Toys, tins, bodies—anything. You lift them, and then—”

His hands opened suddenly.

“Boom,” said the wind in the chimney.

He slid from the chair and crouched behind it.

We waited. The clock resumed its ticking, very gently.

“It’s only the wind,” I said.

“Only the wind,” he repeated, but remained hidden.

Father Time bent beside him. “There are no mines here.”

“Are you certain?”

“As certain as I may be in a writer’s study.”

After a while we coaxed him back into the chair. I wrapped the towel round his shoulders. His clothing smelt of wet earth, smoke, hospitals, horses, and long roads.

“What he requires,” said Time, “is a drink.”

“I have no drink.”

Father Time raised his eyebrows.

“None.”

He looked toward the bottom cupboard.

“That is medicine.”

“Of course. It has been medicine since the first monk put berries into spirits and assured the abbot he had a cough.”

I produced the bottle.

Father Christmas watched the glass being filled. His nostrils stirred. He took one suspicious sip, then a larger one.

“Schnapps?” he asked.

“Brandy.”

“Ah! Brandy!” He swallowed and shut his eyes. “There was a widow near Arras who gave me brandy. Her roof was gone, her two sons were gone, half her village was gone—and still she gave me the bottle she had hidden for winter. ‘You are colder than I am,’ she said.”

“Did it warm you?”

“For an hour.”

He held out the glass.

I filled it again. Warmth began to creep into his face. The fire crackled bravely, performing beyond its means. Father Christmas extended his boots toward it and gave a long sigh.

“That’s better. Oh, that’s better! A hearth! A chair! A roof that stays where a roof ought to stay!”

His gaze travelled about the room: books, pipe-rack, curtains, toy cupboard, family photographs. At the sight of the toys he smiled—faintly at first, as if testing an expression long unused.

Then he saw the broken horse.

“What’s this?”

“My son’s.”

“And you let it lie in that condition?”

“I was occupied with the death of Christmas.”

“Pooh!”

It was not a powerful “Pooh!” but it contained a trace of the old authority. He set down his glass, took up the horse, and turned it expertly in his hands.

“Cracked axle. Loose flank. Mane singed by a candle, I’ll wager.”

“A nursery campaign.”

“There are always campaigns in nurseries, but the casualties should be mended before bedtime.”

From an inner pocket he drew a little roll of tools: awl, pincers, screwdriver, brush, glue-pot, tiny hammer. They were tarnished but immaculate. His fingers, which had shaken at the sound of the wind, became steady over the toy.

“More light, pray.”

I brought the lamp.

“Not in my eyes, man! Here—hold the wheel. No, the other way. Have writers no practical intelligence?”

“Very little. It interferes with criticism.”

He snorted. Father Time chuckled into his beard.

For ten minutes there was peace in the room. The rain softened. The old clock ticked. Father Christmas worked, humming a tune that appeared to know every chimney in Europe. He straightened the axle, fitted the wheel, pressed the split wood together, and bound it with a strip from his own ragged cuff.

“Children,” he said, “are hard on horses. They make them jump over books, charge table legs, and pull loads no sensible animal would attempt. Excellent masters, children.”

“Have you many deliveries this year?” I asked.

The hammer stopped.

His smile vanished.

“Deliveries?”

I regretted the question, but it was too late. He looked at his sack.

“Some.”

He opened it slowly.

There were toys inside, though few were whole. A doll without a face; a trumpet crushed flat; a box of bricks gritted with plaster; a woollen dog scorched along one side. There were also books—dozens of them, swollen by rain, torn by fragments, stained with mud and darker things. Names had been written upon the flyleaves in many hands.

“To Emil, from Mother.”

“For Jeanne, with Papa’s love.”

“To my brave little Stefan.”

“For Lucy, Christmas, 19—”

The year had been burned away.

“I carried them,” said Father Christmas. “Across roads, over fields, through towns with no windows. I came too late. Always too late.”

He lifted the faceless doll.

“This was for a girl in a cellar. She had made a bed for it from a cigar box. The shell came before I did.”

He laid it down and picked up a red picture book.

“A father sent this from the front. He was dead before the parcel left the depot. The boy died in the influenza ward. The book went on travelling. It knew neither of them was waiting.”

“Enough, Nicholas,” Father Time murmured.

“No, he must hear. He says Christmas is dead.”

Father Christmas rose. His new warmth had become fever. He dragged objects from the sack and placed them upon my table like exhibits before a court.

“A skipping rope for a child who lost her legs. A tin engine for two brothers under a fallen wall. A paint-box for a hospital where the windows burst inward. Here—a little wooden flute. The boy played it while the guns were quiet. When the guns began, he played louder. Then the roof—”

His voice failed.

From beyond the house came the grinding of a lorry changing gear. To him it was evidently something else. He dropped flat, covering his head.

“Machine guns!”

“No,” I said. “No, you’re safe.”

“Down! Keep the children down!”

I knelt and touched his shoulder. He fought me blindly, then seized my coat.

“Why do they put children near the guns? Why do they put guns near the children? I took them oranges once. Oranges! Can you remember such folly? Nuts, drums, sugar mice! Now I carry bandages. I fill stockings with bread. I bring candles to cellars so mothers can count who is left.”

His head turned toward the window.

“Do you hear them?”

I heard only the wind, but the wind had found a thin place in the world. Through it came, or seemed to come, voices: a child calling from a station platform, another crying beneath stone, another asking whether Father Christmas could find an address after the street had ceased to exist.

He tore off his cap.

“Give them back!” he cried. “Do you hear me, Time? Give me back my children! The laughing ones, the greedy ones, the solemn ones who write in their best hand! Give me back the child who asks for a kingdom and is satisfied with a whistle. Give me back their beds and their bowls and their mothers’ songs. I cannot go on knocking at empty houses!”

He swayed.

Father Time caught him before he struck the floor. Together we laid him upon the hearth-rug. The broken toys lay around him, a pathetic court of wounded subjects. His face seemed suddenly ancient—not old in Time’s serene fashion, but worn out, used up, ravaged by every winter of the war.

I looked at Father Time.

“Well?” I demanded. “Is this your defence? You have proved my case.”

“No.”

“You brought me Christmas himself, and he is dying.”

“He is suffering.”

“What distinction can matter to him?”

“All distinctions matter to me.”

He covered Father Christmas with my coat and sat beside him.

“You spoke of commerce,” he said. “Yes, greed has often hired musicians and called the noise a carol. You spoke of hypocrisy. Yes, men have given pennies in December and taken pounds in January. You spoke of war. Against that charge I have no jest.”

The room grew paler. Dawn had begun its slow assault upon the curtains.

“But Christmas is not a season supplied by shops,” Time continued. “It is not snow, nor plenty, nor the comfortable remembrance of comforts. It is a compact renewed in darkness—that the helpless shall be sheltered, the hungry invited in, the lonely addressed by name.”

“A compact we have broken.”

“Then renew it.”

“With whom? The dead?”

“With the living first.”

I glanced at Father Christmas. His lips moved. Perhaps he dreamed of sleigh bells; perhaps of guns.

“What can one man do against all that?” I asked.

Father Time’s eyes sharpened.

“That question has excused more wickedness than any lie I know. You cannot silence every gun. You cannot rebuild every school tonight. You cannot restore one child whose little book lies in that sack. Therefore, you conclude, you may do nothing. A comfortable conclusion—and wholly false.”

“What would you have me do?”

“Stand between the children and hatred where you can. Keep from them, for one hour more, the poison that adults drink so eagerly. Tell them courage without teaching cruelty. Let them know sacrifice, but not delight in suffering. Give them games while there is still room to play, songs while there is breath to sing, stories in which mercy is not laughed out of court.”

He pointed to the sack.

“Those gifts failed to arrive. Send others. Food. Books. Kindness. Send letters to children you do not know. Welcome the frightened. Share your fire. And when a small thing is broken, mend it.”

“That will not end the war.”

“No. But it may preserve the world for which the war is said to be fought.”

The first bird called outside—a thin, doubtful note.

“And the dead?” I whispered. “What of them?”

Father Time bowed his head.

“I do not spend lives,” he said. “Men do that, then charge the account to me. Yet I keep what they purchased dearly: lessons, warnings, courage, love. Much is squandered. Much is forgotten. But not all. There may come a day when children now hidden in cellars build houses with broad windows; when men who have heard the guns refuse to point them again; when borders become roads instead of wounds. I promise no easy paradise. I promise only that sacrifice need not be barren if the living make it bear fruit.”

The clock struck six.

At the first stroke, Father Christmas opened his eyes. At the second, he sat up. At the third, he reached for the wooden horse and tightened the binding round its body. At the fourth, he placed it carefully in my hands.

“It will hold,” he said, “if treated kindly.”

At the fifth, the room filled with a grey brightness in which both figures seemed made of breath upon glass.

At the sixth, they were gone.

The chair stood empty. My coat lay folded on the hearth-rug. The bottle was lighter than it had been, which proves nothing supernatural, as my wife later observed. Upon the table remained the damp mark of a sack, but that, too, faded as the fire died.

Only the horse was indisputable.

One wheel turned smoothly. The crack had been drawn together, though the narrow scar remained. Around its body was tied a strip of faded red cloth.

You may say I had fallen asleep at my desk. Very well. I have no wish to quarrel with you before breakfast. A dream may enter without knocking, drink a man’s brandy, rebuke his politics, and leave him with work to do. Reality has often accomplished less.

I sat until the house began to stir. Pipes complained in the walls. A door opened overhead. Small feet crossed the landing, paused, and then came pattering down the stairs.

Before my son reached the study, I took glue, paint, and a little brush from the cupboard. Father Christmas had repaired the axle and bound the crack, but the horse still lacked part of its mane, and there were ugly burns along its flank.

The world also was scorched, split, and short of wheels. I could not mend the world before breakfast.

But I could begin.

So when my son opened the door and asked, “Is he ready?” I set the horse beneath the lamp, drew up my chair, and said:

“Not quite. Come and help me.”

The Clockmaker of Bellwether Street

Every clock in Bellwether stopped at 3:17 on the morning Elias Vale disappeared.

Pocket watches froze in waistcoat drawers. Alarm clocks went silent beside sleeping heads. The great brass clock in the railway station halted between one breath and the next, its minute hand pointing accusingly at the floor. Even the painted wooden rooster above the bakery ceased pecking at the hour.

For seventeen minutes, the town existed without time.

Then, at 3:34, every clock began again.

No one noticed the loss until dawn.

By breakfast, Bellwether was full of people tapping watch faces and comparing times. By noon, the stationmaster had written a report. By evening, Mrs. Vale had unlocked her husband’s shop and found the place empty.

There had been no struggle. Elias’s coat was still hanging behind the door. His spectacles rested on his workbench beside a half-repaired music box. The back window was latched from within, and the shop bell had not rung all night, according to the widow who lived upstairs and slept lightly enough to hear moths strike the glass.

Only two things were missing: Elias himself and the oldest clock in Bellwether.

The clock had no name. It had stood in the back room of the shop for as long as anyone could remember, taller than a man and twice as broad, with a black walnut case carved with moons, stars, foxes, owls, and faces that seemed almost human in poor light. Its dial had thirteen numerals. It never showed the correct hour.

Children dared one another to touch it. Adults pretended not to believe the stories.

Lena Marrow believed them.

She was twelve when Elias vanished and had been his apprentice for six months, though neither of them used that word. Officially, she swept floors, fetched tea, and delivered repaired clocks. Unofficially, Elias had taught her how to straighten a bent pivot without snapping it, how to hear a cracked gear tooth in a running mechanism, and how to hold her breath when lowering a balance spring into place.

“A clock,” he once told her, “is a promise made by metal.”

“A promise to do what?”

“To remember what people forget.”

Now, standing in the empty back room, Lena stared at the pale rectangle on the floorboards where the ancient clock had been.

Mrs. Vale stood behind her, twisting a handkerchief between her fingers.

“The constable says Elias must have left willingly,” she said.

“Without his coat?”

“He says people do strange things.”

“Without his boots?”

Mrs. Vale looked toward the workbench. Beneath it sat Elias’s heavy boots, toes polished by years of wear.

“The constable,” Lena concluded, “is an idiot.”

“Lena.”

“A respectful idiot.”

Mrs. Vale almost smiled, but the smile did not survive. “Go home. Your mother will worry.”

Lena knelt and examined the floor. Four deep grooves marked the boards where the clock’s feet had rested. Dust lay everywhere except in a narrow line leading from the pale rectangle to the blank brick wall.

Not to the door.

To the wall.

She put her palm against the bricks. They were cold enough to hurt.

Behind her, something ticked.

Lena turned.

The clocks in the front room filled the shop with their ordinary chorus: slow ticks, brisk ticks, nervous clicks, the soft whir of escapements. Yet the sound she had heard was different. Deeper. It seemed to come from beneath the floor.

Tick.

She followed it to Elias’s workbench.

Tick.

She opened the top drawer and found brass screws, cleaning cloths, and a heel of bread hardened to stone.

Tick.

The second drawer contained invoices and magnifying lenses.

Tick.

In the bottom drawer, beneath a roll of blue velvet, lay a silver pocket watch.

It was larger than any pocket watch Lena had seen. Its case bore the same carvings as the missing clock: moons, owls, foxes, and tiny faces. There were thirteen numerals on its dial.

Its hands pointed to 3:17.

A scrap of paper had been tied to its chain.

Lena unfolded it.

If the clock takes me, do not follow.

Below this, in smaller letters, Elias had added:

Unless I fail to return before the first snow.

Lena glanced through the shop window. Outside, against a darkening sky, a single white flake drifted down and vanished on the pavement.

Within an hour, snow covered Bellwether Street.

Lena did not go home.

She told Mrs. Vale she would lock the shop, waited for the woman’s footsteps to fade, and carried the silver watch into the back room. The ticking grew louder near the brick wall.

“Do not follow,” she whispered. “That’s a foolish thing to write if you know someone as curious as me.”

The watch sprang open.

Its minute hand began moving backward.

At once, the shop changed.

Shadows lifted from corners and climbed the walls. Dust leapt from the floor into cracks. Lena heard footsteps retreating above her as the widow upstairs walked backward through her rooms. Beyond the window, snow rose from the street in white streams and flew into the clouds.

Time was reversing.

Lena tried to drop the watch, but its chain had wound itself around her wrist.

The bricks before her shivered. Mortar dissolved between them, and one by one they drew apart, revealing a narrow doorway filled with golden light.

On the other side stood the missing clock.

Its pendulum swung in silence.

Lena pulled at the chain. “I changed my mind.”

The watch dragged her forward.

She crossed the threshold, and Bellwether vanished behind her.

She landed on a road paved with clock faces.

Around her stretched a city under a motionless violet sky. Towers rose at impossible angles, their windows bright with trapped sunsets. Bridges curved upward and ended in midair. Thousands of clocks hung from iron trees, chiming hours that had never existed. Along the road hurried people in clothes from different ages: a soldier in rusted armor, a woman carrying a glass umbrella, a barefoot boy with flowers growing from his hair.

None cast shadows.

At the roadside, a sign pointed in three directions.

YESTERDAY

TOO LATE

THE THIRTEENTH HOUR

Someone cleared his throat.

A fox sat beneath the sign. He wore a green waistcoat, and a pair of spectacles balanced on his narrow muzzle.

“You are not Elias Vale,” he said.

“You’re a fox.”

“Neither observation is particularly useful.”

Lena stared at him.

The fox took out a tiny watch and consulted it. “You are early, late, and precisely where you should not be. Very inconvenient.”

“Where is Elias?”

“Taken.”

“By whom?”

“The Keeper.”

“Where?”

The fox pointed toward the tallest tower in the city. It was black, windowless, and crowned by a clock with thirteen hands.

“There.”

Lena began walking.

The fox trotted after her. “I would not do that.”

“You’re welcome to stay here.”

“I would, but you have something belonging to me.”

She looked at the silver watch chained to her wrist.

“This?”

“Once. Long ago. Before your town was built, before your language learned the word Tuesday, before humans decided minutes should all be the same length.”

“Minutes are the same length.”

The fox laughed so hard he had to sit down.

Lena continued toward the tower.

The city grew stranger as she entered it. In one square, rain fell upward from a fountain. In another, old men played cards with their younger selves. Shop windows displayed bottled summers, lost opportunities, and final words that had never been spoken. At a market stall, a masked merchant sold small parcels labeled AN AFTERNOON YOU THOUGHT WOULD LAST FOREVER.

Lena kept her eyes on the tower.

“What is this place?” she asked.

“The place between moments,” said the fox. “Discarded time collects here.”

“And the Keeper?”

“Collects the rest.”

“Why did he take Elias?”

“Because your clockmaker tried to steal a day.”

Lena stopped. “Elias never stole anything.”

“All clockmakers steal. They cut eternity into pieces and sell it by the hour.”

“That sounds clever, but it isn’t an answer.”

The fox’s ears tilted back. “Your master came here to bargain. His wife is ill.”

Lena knew Mrs. Vale had been weak throughout autumn. Elias had often closed the shop early to take her home, though Mrs. Vale insisted it was only a stubborn cold.

“He wanted more time for her,” Lena said.

“He wanted the day on which she died removed from the calendar. The Keeper dislikes such requests.”

“Then why didn’t Elias come back?”

“Because the Keeper made him a better offer.”

They reached the tower at midnight, though the sky had not changed. Its door was made from black wood and had no handle.

Thirteen keyholes surrounded its frame.

Lena examined them. “Do you have a key?”

“I have several. None for this.”

She took Elias’s watch from her apron pocket—the ordinary watch he used while working. She had found it beside his spectacles and carried it without thinking. Its winding key was fixed to the chain.

The key fit the smallest keyhole.

She turned it.

Something vast shifted inside the tower.

The door opened.

Beyond it lay Elias’s shop.

For one hopeful instant, Lena thought she had returned to Bellwether. Then she saw hundreds of Eliases seated at hundreds of benches, all working beneath cold blue lamps.

One Elias was a child. Another had white hair to his waist. One had mechanical hands. One was no more than a shadow. Each repaired a different clock, and every clock showed 3:17.

In the center of the room stood the real Elias, bent over the ancient walnut clock.

“Elias!”

He looked up.

A smile of relief crossed his tired face, followed at once by horror.

“Lena, no.”

She ran to him. “You said not to follow unless it snowed.”

“I wrote that before I knew what the snow meant.”

“What does it mean?”

“That no time is passing in Bellwether.”

Lena remembered snow rising from the street as the watch turned backward.

“How long have you been here?” she asked.

“Perhaps a day. Perhaps forty years.” Elias touched her shoulder as if making sure she was real. “The Keeper stopped our town when I crossed over. Bellwether is trapped inside the missing seventeen minutes.”

“But the clocks started again.”

“Their hands did. Time did not.”

Lena thought of everyone in town waking, eating breakfast, arguing at the station, and going home. “That’s impossible.”

“People often continue after time stops. Habit is a powerful spring.”

The fox jumped onto a workbench. “Charming reunion. We should now discuss escape.”

Every lamp in the room went out.

A thirteenth chime sounded.

The Keeper stepped from inside the walnut clock.

He was tall and dressed in a coat stitched from calendar pages. Instead of a face, he wore a polished brass dial. Two black hands turned slowly across it, though there were no numerals to indicate what they measured.

When he spoke, his voice came from every clock in the room.

“Elias Vale. You have brought me an apprentice.”

“I brought no one,” Elias said.

“Everyone brings those who love them.”

Lena stepped between them, although her knees had begun to shake. “Let him go.”

The hands on the Keeper’s face paused.

“You possess eighty-one years, seven months, two days, and some scattered hours,” he said. “You offer commands as though you possess more.”

“I offer a bargain.”

Elias seized her arm. “No.”

The Keeper turned toward her. “What do you seek?”

“Mrs. Vale lives. Bellwether goes free. Elias and I go home.”

“And what do you offer?”

Lena had expected this question, but now that it had come, she found her plans embarrassingly thin.

“I can repair your clock.”

The hundreds of Eliases stopped working.

The Keeper’s coat rustled.

“My clock is not broken.”

“Yes, it is.”

Elias stared at her. “Lena—”

She pointed to the ancient clock’s pendulum. It swung left, then right, but the movement was subtly uneven. The rightward arc was shorter.

“You’ve had hundreds of versions of Elias working on clocks showing 3:17,” she said. “You trapped Bellwether at that minute. You took the old clock because it’s connected to the town. But you still can’t make the missing seventeen minutes hold properly.”

The Keeper’s face hands began to turn faster.

The fox whispered, “Careful.”

Lena continued. “You don’t collect discarded time. You’re losing it.”

A crack appeared across the brass dial where the Keeper’s mouth might have been.

From inside his coat came a sound like distant thunder.

“Time cannot be lost.”

“Then why are you afraid?”

The room shook. Clocks fell from shelves, striking the floor without breaking. The many Eliases flickered.

The real Elias leaned close. “You’re right,” he whispered. “The clock has been slowing ever since I arrived. But I could not find the fault.”

Lena studied the mechanism. The walnut case stood open. Within it, gears turned in glittering layers, far deeper than the case should have allowed. Some were the size of coins; others seemed as vast as moons.

“A clock is a promise made by metal,” she murmured.

The fox’s ears rose. “And what promise did this one make?”

Lena looked at the carvings: moons, stars, owls, foxes, and human faces. She saw then that the faces were not decorations. One resembled Mrs. Vale. Another looked like Elias. A third looked disturbingly like Lena.

“It promised to remember,” she said.

The Keeper raised one long hand. “Enough.”

His fingers closed.

The room froze.

The falling clocks hung in midair. Elias stood motionless beside Lena. Even her heartbeat stopped, yet somehow she remained conscious.

Only the fox moved.

He leapt from the bench and bit the Keeper’s ankle.

The Keeper cried out in twelve voices.

Time crashed back into motion.

“Run!” shouted the fox.

Lena did not run. She plunged both hands into the clock.

Cold shot through her fingers. The gears were not metal. One contained the smell of rain on Bellwether Street. Another held the sound of Mrs. Vale laughing. A silver wheel flashed with Lena’s memory of her father lifting her onto his shoulders when she was five. Each piece was a moment, cut and polished until it fit beside another.

Then she saw the fault.

At the heart of the mechanism was an empty space.

Not a broken gear. A missing memory.

“Elias!” she shouted. “What happened at 3:17?”

He ducked as the Keeper swept an arm across the bench. “What?”

“The clock remembers the town. Something happened at 3:17 that it can’t remember.”

The Keeper seized the fox by the tail and flung him into a cabinet.

Elias stared at the mechanism. “At 3:17, I crossed the threshold.”

“That isn’t all.”

“I started the clock.”

“Why then?”

“Because—”

His face changed.

Mrs. Vale had appeared at the tower door.

She wore only a nightdress beneath her winter cloak. Snow dusted her hair, and in one hand she carried a kitchen knife.

“I told you,” she said breathlessly, “that I am not dying.”

Elias went pale. “Mara?”

“You left a note claiming you had gone to save my life. That is not a note any sensible wife can ignore.”

The Keeper released a shriek of grinding machinery.

The entire tower leaned.

Mrs. Vale gripped the doorframe. “I woke at 3:17 the night before Elias left,” she called. “He was sitting beside me, holding that silver watch.”

Elias closed his eyes.

“I asked him what was wrong,” she continued. “He said nothing. He always says nothing when he means everything.”

Lena reached deeper into the clock’s mechanism. “What happened next?”

“I told him I knew the doctor’s diagnosis. I told him I had perhaps a month. Elias promised I would not die.”

The empty space within the mechanism began to glow.

“And you?” Lena asked. “What did you promise?”

Mrs. Vale looked at her husband.

“I promised not to forgive him if he wasted our last month searching for a miracle.”

The missing gear appeared in Lena’s hands.

It was small, warm, and made of no metal she knew. Along its edge were engraved two words:

LET GO.

The Keeper lunged.

Elias threw himself into the Keeper’s path. They struck the floor together. Calendar pages tore from the Keeper’s coat and whirled through the room: winters, birthdays, wars, quiet Sundays, afternoons not yet lived.

“Now, Lena!” Elias shouted.

She placed the gear into the empty space.

It fit perfectly.

The clock struck 3:18.

The sound shattered the tower.

Walls split open, revealing the violet sky. Bridges uncurled over the rooftops. Bottled summers burst in the streets below, flooding the city with sunlight. The hundreds of Eliases vanished one after another, each giving Lena a brief nod before fading.

The Keeper staggered upright. A crack divided his brass face.

“You have released what cannot be restored,” he said.

“No,” Lena replied. “I released what you couldn’t keep.”

The clock struck 3:19.

Wind tore the calendar coat from the Keeper’s body. Beneath it, he was small, ancient, and terribly human.

The clock struck 3:20.

The city dissolved.

Lena felt Elias grab one hand and Mrs. Vale the other. The fox caught her apron in his teeth. Together they were lifted into a storm of ticking, chiming, ringing sound.

For one instant, Lena saw every clock in Bellwether at once.

Then she fell onto the floor of the shop.

Morning sunlight streamed through the windows.

Outside, carts rolled along Bellwether Street, leaving tracks in fresh snow. The railway clock chimed seven. Somewhere, a baby began to cry, and somewhere else, someone burned the first batch of breakfast rolls.

Time had resumed.

Mrs. Vale sat against the wall, laughing and weeping. Elias knelt beside her.

The ancient clock stood in its old place, its pendulum swinging evenly. Its dial now had twelve numerals.

The silver watch lay open on the floor. Its hands moved normally.

The fox was gone.

For a while, no one spoke.

Then Mrs. Vale slapped Elias.

It was not a hard slap, but it echoed impressively through the shop.

“That,” she said, “is for bargaining away forty years of your life without consulting me.”

Lena blinked. “Forty years?”

Elias touched his cheek. “The Keeper’s first offer.”

Mrs. Vale slapped him again.

“And that is for leaving a note.”

“I thought the note was clear.”

“It said, ‘Gone to correct an error. Back soon.’”

“I was under pressure.”

Lena began to laugh. She laughed until she had to sit on the floor. After a moment, Mrs. Vale joined her. Even Elias smiled.

The doctor had been correct. Mrs. Vale lived twenty-seven more days.

They were not miraculous days. She slept often. She suffered. There were medicines, difficult mornings, and long nights when the house seemed to hold its breath. But there were also shared meals, music from the repaired music box, and afternoons when sunlight filled the upstairs room.

Elias did not search for another doorway.

On the final evening, snow began falling over Bellwether. Mrs. Vale asked him to open the window.

“It’s cold,” he protested.

“That is how winter works.”

He opened it.

Lena sat beside the bed while Mrs. Vale watched the snow. The town clocks began striking nine, never quite together.

“Untidy,” Mrs. Vale whispered.

“Elias says no two clocks agree because each remembers a different world,” Lena said.

“Elias says many things when he wants to avoid admitting his repairs are imperfect.”

From downstairs came his offended voice. “I heard that.”

Mrs. Vale smiled.

She died sometime after midnight, holding her husband’s hand. No clocks stopped. No thunder sounded. The universe did not break.

A single moment ended, and the next began.

Years later, when Elias’s hands grew too unsteady for delicate work, the sign above the shop changed from VALE, CLOCKMAKER to MARROW & VALE. Later still, it read simply LENA MARROW, HOROLOGIST.

The ancient clock remained in the back room. It kept excellent time, though every winter, on the first snowy night, it lost seventeen minutes.

Lena never corrected it.

Sometimes customers asked about the carved fox in its walnut case. It seemed an odd detail, especially with the tiny green waistcoat and spectacles.

Lena would smile and say it had always been there.

This was not entirely true.

On quiet evenings, when the town settled and all the repaired clocks spoke softly to one another, she sometimes heard claws crossing the back room. In the morning, a muddy paw print would mark the floor, and the silver watch would be wound though she had left it untouched.

Once, many years after the missing seventeen minutes, Lena found a parcel on her workbench.

Inside was a tiny brass gear and a folded note.

The note read:

Minutes are not the same length.

You were right about everything else.

Lena laughed, placed the gear in her parts drawer, and opened the shop for another day.

Outside, Bellwether hurried through rain, weddings, market mornings, funerals, missed trains, first kisses, last words, and all the other hours people imagined they could keep.

Above them, the railway clock struck eight.

For once, every clock in town struck with it.

Then one small watch hesitated, remembered something better, and fell a second behind.
